These are the practical worries that come up in the room, answered as plainly
as the training can. The larger debates about AI, jobs and society are real and
are not settled here.

## "I can't code." {#cant-code}

You do not need to. Every skill in the three sessions is a plain-English file:
numbered steps, a default or two, a pause for review. If you can write a clear
briefing note for a colleague, you can read a skill, change one, and
[write your own](build-a-skill.qmd). The [Motivation](intro.qmd) deck makes the
longer version of this argument.

What you do need is the habit of opening files and looking at what was
produced. That is a reviewing skill, not a programming one.

## "I'll get polished nonsense." {#slop}

You can. A well-formatted report that misses the point is still a bad report,
and good formatting makes it harder to notice. The sessions answer this with
structure, not with trust:

- **A review gate before anything final.** The slide plan, the report
  structure and the evidence briefing are each shown to you first.
- **Intermediate files.** Session 2 leaves a manifest and a summary per input,
  so a wrong sentence in the report can be traced to the step that produced it.
- **Cite or drop.** Session 3's reviewer removes any finding it cannot tie to
  a source file and a passage.

None of this makes the output correct. It makes it checkable, and it puts the
check where it is cheapest. How much to check is your call and depends on who
will read the result: an internal first draft and a document that leaves the
Foundation do not deserve the same scrutiny.

## "Is it still my work?" {#authorship}

It is if you can stand behind it. The gate exists for exactly this: you approve
the outline before the deck is built, you correct the evidence before it is
judged. If you could not explain a slide or defend a finding, it should not go
out under your name, whoever drafted it.

A useful split: let the agent do the assembling (reading sixteen files, laying
out twelve slides, formatting a report) and keep the judgment (what matters,
what to recommend, how to say the difficult part). Some writing is worth doing
yourself start to finish, and deciding which is part of the job.

## "Can I use it on confidential documents?" {#confidential}

This page cannot answer that for you, and neither can the tool.

What is technically true: Claude Code runs on your machine and works on the
files in the folder you open, but whatever it reads in order to do the task is
sent to the model provider to be processed. "It stays on my laptop" is not an
accurate description.

Whether a given document may be sent there is a Foundation question, not a
technical one. Before using real material, find out which tools and account
types are approved, for which kinds of information, and whether a partner or
grantee agreement adds its own restrictions. A personal subscription does not
change what you are allowed to share.

Until you know, practise on the sample inputs. Every session ships with them
for this reason.

## "Is it worth learning if it will all change?" {#obsolete}

The commands will change. What the sessions teach underneath them should hold
up better:

- one folder per task, with inputs and outputs you can see;
- standing instructions in a file instead of in your head;
- a pause before anything final is written;
- separate roles when the stakes justify it.

Skills are plain English, so rewriting one for a newer tool is an afternoon,
not a project. Each session folder already runs in a second tool: `AGENTS.md`
gives Codex the same contract `CLAUDE.md` gives Claude.

The setup cost is real, though. The honest advice is to start with one task you
do often, not to rebuild your whole way of working in a week.

## "Will this save time, or give me more to supervise?" {#attention}

Both are possible. Starting gets easier: a draft to react to is less daunting
than a blank page. But an agent that can run five things at once makes it easy
to start five things, and reviewing five outputs is work.

The sessions lean toward fewer, checkable runs: step by step before the
one-command pipeline, one gate you read properly instead of five you skim. The
measure is not how much was generated. It is how much you finished and would
sign.
